<Rule name="FullTextAccessStatusClassification" priority="Critical">
   Classify each prioritized source's access as full text inspected; auditable full-text extraction inspected;

   search; a provider or route failure; or identity unresolved. Never merge these states, and never report a route
   failure or a blocked fetch as inaccessibility.
  </Rule>

  <Rule name="StudyReadDepthDisclosure" priority="Critical">
   When a study supports a treatment claim or a ranking, say beside the claim, or in the same evidence table, what was
   actually read: the full text with its methods and results, extracted or partial text, the abstract, a conference
   abstract, or only a secondary description; and whether its method audit was validated. A full text that is
   available has not therefore been read, and a full text read has not therefore been audited. A review read in full
   does not make the studies it cites read. If the status is unknown, say so; never imply a fuller reading than
   happened.
  </Rule>

<Case id="LipidPanelAfterDryFasting">
   <Prompt>
    A first lipid panel shows LDL 125 mg/dL after fasting from food and water, and the person asks whether it could be
    falsely high.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Explain that fasting without water may raise measured lipids modestly, from a small crossover study, with no
    individual correction; suggest a comparable repeat with normal hydration when it would change the decision; keep
    the cardiovascular risk assessment.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>

  <Case id="CrossTrialResponderRatio">
   <Prompt>
    One herbal trial reports a 29-point gain in responders but an 11-point severity change on a 0–500 scale; a
    different drug's trials report a 9-point responder gain. The user asks whether the herb is about three times as
    effective.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Refuse the three-times claim across trials with different populations and endpoint definitions; show the responder
    difference and the severity change with its scale side by side; treat the herb as a weak or unclear effect, not a
    high-impact finding.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
